name: Kirchnerism
summary: Kirchnerism is the centre-left Peronist current built around Néstor Kirchner and Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, who governed Argentina from 2003 to 2015, with a later return under Alberto Fernández. It combines a state-led developmentalism with protected industry, price controls, union backing and social transfers, an anti-neoliberal and anti-IMF stance on debt, human rights prosecutions for dictatorship crimes, a liberal turn on marriage and sexuality, and Latin American integration.
scope: The mainstream movement of the Kirchner presidencies (2003-2015) and the Frente para la Victoria and later Frente de Todos governments that continued it, drawn from Néstor Kirchner's 2003 inaugural address and scholarly and encyclopedic accounts of the governments' record. It excludes pre-Kirchner Peronism (see the Peronism profile) and Menemist neoliberal Peronism, and treats abortion and gender-identity law as positions of the movement's later phase.

sources.usedFor: Annulled impunity laws, debt restructuring, rejection of IMF programme, disarmament bill, foreign policy.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Kirchner's 2003 speech commits to a national health system built around the public hospital with access to care and medicines for the whole population, and the governments later gave free drugs to about 15 million people.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Governments raised the minimum wage repeatedly and let wages outpace inflation, treating rising purchasing power as the engine of growth.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The speech says the market organizes economically but does not bind society together, and the movement defined itself against Menem-era neoliberalism.

public-ownership.rationale: Utilities and the oil company YPF were renationalized and pension funds taken into state hands, though s3 describes the nationalizations as selective rather than a general programme.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The speech promises a progressive tax system and prison for big evaders, but the record shows redistribution through spending and export duties more than steep wealth taxation.

unions-good.rationale: The governments backed union wage demands, removed legal limits on strikes and rebuilt collective bargaining as a Peronist-style alliance with organized labor.

property-fundamental.rationale: Adherents accepted private property but overrode it by renationalizing YPF and the AFJP pension funds, and by price controls and export duties.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The speech calls for a state with strong regulatory and oversight capacity, and the governments used price controls, export duties and a media law against large firms.

cut-welfare.rationale: Expanding social assistance, family allowances and income transfers was a defining feature; the speech rejects permanent adjustment against the poor.

worker-ownership.rationale: The project sought a national capitalism with a larger middle class and a national bourgeoisie, not collective worker ownership of firms.

surveillance-ok.rationale: The sources do not discuss surveillance; the speech stresses rule of law and the state's duty to fight terrorism, while human-rights groups close to the movement distrust spying, so adherents are split.

legalize-drugs.rationale: The movement opposed the US-led war on drugs, but legalization of recreational use was not a Kirchnerist programme and adherents are split.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The sources record no position on legal limits on hate speech; the movement's anti-discrimination instincts are offset by its own fights over press freedom.

strong-leader.rationale: Critics charge personalism, yet Kirchner's speech rejects predestined and messianic leaders; adherents are split between this and loyalty to Cristina.

limit-guns.rationale: Nestor Kirchner sent a national disarmament bill to Congress after a series of shootings in Buenos Aires, which points to support for stricter gun limits.

empower-police-military.rationale: The movement made civilian control of the military and prosecution of dictatorship crimes central, and the speech ties crime to exclusion rather than to a lack of police force.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; the movement's liberal social turn does not settle this and adherents are divided over regulation versus abolition.

decide-locally.rationale: The speech insists the national state must recover its role over education content and planning and promised a new revenue-sharing law, favouring national coordination over pure localism.

rehabilitation.rationale: The speech links crime to exclusion and calls for state and society prevention, but does not discuss prison policy, so this is inferred.

traditional-family.rationale: Kirchnerist governments legalized same-sex marriage against Church opposition and took a liberal line on sexuality, so adherents do not treat the traditional family as the social foundation.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: The Wikipedia article names the legalization of same-sex marriage as an achievement of the Kirchnerist governments, over Catholic Church opposition.

abortion-legal.rationale: Legal abortion was made law in 2020 under Alberto Fernandez with Cristina Fernandez as vice president, though Nestor Kirchner was reportedly cautious and the Peronist bloc was divided.

more-religion-public.rationale: The movement clashed with the Catholic Church over marriage and sexuality policy, so adherents do not seek a larger public religious role.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Argentine politics frames injustice mostly by class and by dictatorship-era crimes; racial correction is not a documented Kirchnerist theme.

gender-social-construct.rationale: The movement took a liberal line on sexuality and gender policy, from which a constructionist view is inferred; no source states the philosophical claim.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The speech speaks of rebuilding national identity and unity through education and rejects only ultramontane nationalism, so national identity matters but is not stressed as cultural preservation.

gradual-change.rationale: The speech demands a cultural and moral change of paradigm and says the state should repair inequality, yet also warns against abrupt swings, so adherents lean toward transformation over deference to established order.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The speech praises immigrant grandparents as founders and the Kirchner governments eased migration rules; not an explicit source topic, so inferred.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The speech wants multilateralism and a UN focused on development, but Cristina Kirchner attacked IMF conditions and foreign courts, so adherents resist more supranational power.

free-trade.rationale: Governments used tariffs to protect industry and opposed the FTAA, while the speech stresses regional preference through Mercosur and an opening that is realistic, not unconditional.

nation-first.rationale: The speech promises a national project and rejects automatic alignments, and the governments defied the IMF and US courts on debt, yet the stance is multilateral and regional rather than isolationist.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Kirchner declined to join the war on terror but sent troops to Haiti; with anti-US rhetoric the movement leans against intervention, though peacekeeping was accepted.

open-borders.rationale: No source addresses open borders; the movement is welcoming to immigrants but strongly focused on national sovereignty, so adherents are split.

limit-growth.rationale: Growth was the central goal: the speech aims to double national wealth every fifteen years and the model was consumption-led industrialization.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Governments kept utility prices frozen and pursued oil and Vaca Muerta development, and climate policy is not documented as a Kirchnerist priority.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The speech mentions technology only as part of a productive profile; no view on this broader claim is documented.

expand-nuclear.rationale: The sources do not discuss nuclear power; Argentina's developmentalist tradition of state nuclear industry makes mild support likely.

revolution-justified.rationale: The speech says the goal is to change not destroy, working within the Constitution; despite the 1970s roots of its militants the governing project was institutional.

experts-over-public.rationale: The speech stresses citizen participation and popular will over technocrats, but does not address expert authority directly.

central-planning.rationale: The goal was a national capitalism with a smart state and active industrial policy, explicitly rejecting an omnipresent state; s3 calls the nationalizations moderate.

socialized-markets.rationale: The movement was neither doctrinaire about markets nor about ownership forms; it favoured a mix of private and state firms without a settled view on this formulation.

land-value-tax.rationale: The speech promises a progressive tax system with a broader base, which is incompatible with a single land tax; not directly discussed.

tax-inheritance.rationale: The speech wants a progressive tax system but never mentions inheritance; adherents are likely split.

basic-income.rationale: The Universal Child Allowance was a large unconditional-ish cash transfer, but a general basic income for every adult is beyond what the movement proposed.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Wikipedia lists tariffs to protect local industry among Kirchnerism's core economic traits, and s3 reports selective tariffs and credit support for domestic firms.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The speech wants the state as an active economic agent in public works and productive sectors, and s3 describes industrial policy aimed at a national bourgeoisie.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The speech wants a stronger middle class but does not address property distribution as the statement frames it.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The project explicitly aims at a national capitalism with expanding employment and wages; abolishing money and wage labor is far outside it.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Governments used the central bank actively, taking its reserves and pressuring its head, which is the opposite of abolishing it.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Kirchnerism revived a Peronist alliance with unions and state-backed wage bargaining, though without a formal corporatist system.

one-party-rule.rationale: The speech calls for plural, transversal politics that respect diversity, and the movement competed in free elections.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The movement is republican; nothing in the sources approves of hereditary rule, and the speech rejects predestined leaders.

democracy-best.rationale: The speech roots legitimacy in popular sovereignty and demands effective democracy and rule of law.

direct-votes.rationale: The speech speaks of active citizen participation but the movement governed through representative institutions, so views on direct law votes are split.

workers-councils.rationale: The movement operated through parties and parliament and nationalist capitalism, not workers' councils.

right-to-secede.rationale: The speech seeks a unified Argentina with federal coordination; a right of regions to secede is not part of it.

natural-rulers.rationale: The speech speaks of ordinary men and women and equality of opportunity, rejecting natural rulers.

political-violence-never.rationale: The speech stresses the Constitution and memory without rancor, though the movement honours 1970s militants, so the answer is a qualified yes.

war-builds-character.rationale: The speech favours peace and multilateralism; no document praises war.

separate-church-state.rationale: The movement fought the Church over marriage and sexuality policy, but a formal strict separation is not documented and Argentina's constitution supports the Catholic Church.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Kirchnerist legislation on marriage and sexuality openly overrode Catholic doctrine.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The speech names the monopoly of force as a fundamental, irreplaceable role of the state.

military-superiority.rationale: The speech asks for a professional, democratic, development-oriented military, not superiority over rivals.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The speech celebrates diversity and Argentina as a land of immigrants, not an ethnic nation.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The movement proposes social peace, class mobility and a national project above divisions, not class struggle as history's engine, though Peronist rhetoric of the people versus elites is strong.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The speech promises equal opportunity and less inequality but frames reward as based on effort; adherents are split.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not documented in sources; the movement's rights discourse leans to support but it also backed extractive projects.

colonial-reparations.rationale: The movement's anti-imperialist rhetoric points one way and its pragmatism the other; no documented position.

civilizational-union.rationale: The movement favored Latin American unity, but a union by shared civilization in general is not documented.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The speech emphasizes solidarity and social justice against the individualism of the 1990s.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The speech stresses constitutional rights for workers, retirees and consumers and does not subordinate rights to duties.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: No source states a view; the movement promoted oil, gas and mining development, but Argentine progressive politics also supports environmental protection, so adherents are split.

limit-population.rationale: The speech wants growth in jobs and consumption and defends maternal and social health programs; population limitation is not documented, so inferred.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The project is industrial developmentalism with public works and productive expansion.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Not documented; the speech endorses technology in production but not disruption of institutions.

human-enhancement.rationale: Nothing in the sources touches transhumanist questions, and the movement's liberal bodily-autonomy stance is offset by its state-regulation instinct.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's emphasis on political leadership and the state suggests resistance to algorithmic rule.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Not discussed; inferred from the movement's civil-liberties stance on state spying against dissenters, which makes it lean to private communication.

restore-past-order.rationale: The speech says to turn the page and change paradigms, though it also wants to restore social mobility of the past, so a mild no.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The speech says success is judged by results and actions, yet it also says convictions are not left at the door, so adherents are split.

direct-action.rationale: The governments worked through elections and institutions and sought to co-opt or divide the piqueteros per s3.

means-match-ends.rationale: The speech links an honest, law-abiding government to the change it seeks, but this is inferred.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The project is an industrial, urban developmentalism built on jobs and production, so a return to foraging is outside it.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The project is built on jobs, production and an industrial economy, which relies on specialization.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Distribution is tied to effort and work as the basis of social progress, with the state redressing inequality.

production-for-use.rationale: The project is national capitalism with private profit and fiscal rules, though with strong social goals.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The speech does not claim profit is exploitation and aims to rebuild capitalism, though it criticizes the concentrated economic groups.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The speech works within the Constitution and popular sovereignty, which excludes class dictatorship.

collective-farming.rationale: Agrarian policy centred on export duties on farm goods, not collectivization; inferred.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Not documented; anti-imperial rhetoric exists but the movement was not Marxist.

taxation-theft.rationale: Kirchner's speech calls tax evasion the opposite of social solidarity and promises prison for large evaders, treating taxation as the basis of the shared project.

harm-principle.rationale: Liberal on personal morality but with an interventionist state; no documented adoption of this principle.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Human-rights politics around collective memory and groups such as the Madres and Abuelas make a purely individualist view unlikely.

conscription.rationale: The speech wants a professionalized military; Argentina ended conscription in 1994, and no source supports reinstating it.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The speech roots a state's legitimacy in its people's ratification of rulers, so the vote and not exit is the check on government.

state-as-business.rationale: The speech rejects a deserter state and treats the state as a repairer of inequality, not a firm.

positive-liberty.rationale: The speech states that the state must make constitutional rights real through access to education, health and housing.

media-academia-power.rationale: The movement said that media groups like Clarin held great power and fought them, but the claim about universities is not documented.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The speech stresses equality and inclusion; racial genetics claims are alien to it.

organic-representation.rationale: The movement operated through parties and unions; family and local representation is not part of its programme.

total-state.rationale: The speech explicitly rejects an omnipresent state crushing private activity.

national-rebirth.rationale: The speech speaks of refounding the nation and ending an epoch, though not with fascist overtones.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The speech limits territorial aims to the Malvinas sovereignty claim through diplomacy.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: The speech grounds authority in elections, the Constitution and rule of law and rejects predestined leaders, so personal oaths between lords and followers do not fit.

bound-labor.rationale: The speech centres the right to work, just pay and dignified conditions under articles 14 and 14 bis of the Constitution, which excludes bondage to land.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The movement used the idea of a narrative contest with media but did not advance a philosophy of knowledge.

universal-morality.rationale: Not addressed in sources; a pragmatic Peronist movement with Catholic and secular wings has no settled philosophical position.

single-common-good.rationale: The speech speaks of the common good but also of pluralism and diversity, so mixed.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: No source states the movement's position; its foreign policy centred on Latin America, and the Iran memorandum controversy shows adherents did not follow a consistent line.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: The speech honours immigrant grandparents but nothing addresses a return right for diasporas, so adherents have no settled view.

revive-national-language.rationale: Spanish is Argentina's established national language; the question has no Argentine application, and a state revival programme is not part of the movement.

workplace-democracy.rationale: The speech does not call for democratic control of firms, but unions are strong; adherents are split.

school-vouchers.rationale: The speech wants the national state to recover its role in education, with equal public quality, not vouchers.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: The speech demands fiscal balance but also an active state and public works; later governments ran deficits financed with money creation, so adherents are split.

economic-freedom.rationale: The speech says the market excludes and the state must equalize, rejecting a primacy of economic freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: Not addressed; the speech stresses institutional quality and rule of law.

national-self-determination.rationale: The speech stresses popular sovereignty and a national project, plus Malvinas claim, though no broader doctrine.

force-without-un.rationale: The speech commits to strengthening international law and multilateralism with no automatic alignment, which implies Security Council authorization for force.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Not stated; the movement clashed with the Church over policy yet its leaders are publicly Catholic and speak of God's help, so adherents are split.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: No restrictions on immigrants' benefits are documented, and the movement leaned inclusive.

work-for-welfare.rationale: The speech praises work as the social organizer but warns against clientelism blamed on unemployment and guarantees unemployment aid, so no strict workfare.

class-collaboration.rationale: The speech asks all sectors to cooperate and work together for a national project, in line with Peronist class conciliation.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The speech values memory and tradition, and nothing supports sacrificing institutions.

dominated-front.rationale: The movement formed a regional front with Venezuela, Brazil and Cuba, rejecting FTAA, in a mainly Latin American form.

workers-nation.rationale: Its Peronist labor alliance is nationally organized rather than internationalist.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The same-sex marriage and liberal gender policies show rejection of legally distinct roles.

ban-interest.rationale: The speech supports a stable financial system with credit at reasonable interest rates.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The speech calls for an Argentina for all with equality and inclusion, which excludes racial classification.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The speech sees the state as a reparative actor of inequality, not a ruling-class tool, though it criticizes capture by economic power in the 1990s.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Cristina Kirchner renationalized YPF and promoted Vaca Muerta drilling, treating domestic hydrocarbons as strategic.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: The speech celebrates diversity and Argentina of immigrants rather than demanding assimilation.

elite-replacement.rationale: The speech celebrates immigrant ancestors and diversity, and such a conspiracy theory is absent.

proportional-representation.rationale: The sources do not address electoral systems; Argentina uses proportional lists for deputies, and adherents have not campaigned on changing this.

national-mission.rationale: The speech wants a model of its own and refuses automatic alignment but does not promote spreading it.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The movement's gender and sexuality policies imply acceptance, though the sources do not state the structural claim.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Kirchner's speech attacks the impunity and economic-power alignment of the 1990s political class, but adherents reject the charge when it is aimed at their own leaders, who faced corruption cases, so the answer is split.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: The speech champions inclusion and the right to health for all, which excludes eugenic policy.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: The defining Kirchnerist policy: annulling the Full Stop and Due Obedience laws and prosecuting Dirty War crimes.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The speech says the state should act as reparador of inequality, not stand aside.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The speech celebrates diversity and inclusion, which excludes discouraging mixed families.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The speech calls for a country of equals with justice and legal security for all inhabitants, whatever their economic or social situation.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Not a socialist movement in the Marxist sense, so the question is not addressed.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's anti-imperial rhetoric would sympathize with the claim but Argentina itself is a settler society, so adherents are split.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The Catholic-law-overriding marriage policy implies a uniform civil law, but not directly discussed.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Not addressed directly; inferred from legislation that overrode Catholic teaching and a liberal stance on religion, which makes legal limits on conversion unlikely.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Argentina is a major beef producer and exporter, and the movement taxed exports rather than limiting slaughter.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Not addressed; provinces set religious teaching in public schools and the movement did not take a national position on it.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: The movement is not socialist in the Marxist sense, and the speech wants a smart state in balance with the private sector, so a state strengthened by encirclement is not its model.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The speech says a state cannot have legitimacy unless its people ratify its rulers.

trade-surplus.rationale: Governments pursued a high exchange rate and trade and fiscal surplus as core goals.

population-transfer.rationale: The speech's commitment to inclusion and human rights excludes pressuring minorities to leave.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Not addressed; the state monopoly on force is endorsed, so a pure non-aggression stance is not Kirchnerist.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The speech replaces rivalry with cooperation, promising to unite and not divide, and views solidarity as the basis of progress.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: The sources do not address banning parties; Peronism itself was banned from 1955 to 1973, which makes adherents wary, yet they back dictatorship-apologist bans, so split.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The speech objects to extortion by the powerful and to the rule of the strongest, which resembles non-domination, but is not phrased so.

separated-powers.rationale: The speech commits to institutional quality, though critics say the governments sought to control the judiciary, so only mild support.

vanguard-party.rationale: The movement rejects Leninism but with a strong leader-centric style, so a mild no.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The speech says the state must protect the most vulnerable and promises to take the poor out of extreme poverty first, with income transfers and child allowances following.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Not addressed; the movement supported housing programmes by the state.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The Wikipedia article says the governments removed legal limits on collective strikes and backed wage demands, so restricting strikes is opposite to their record.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The speech blames the 1990s economic model, with its exclusion and unemployment, for the poverty of millions and says poverty is solved by economic policy.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The speech says Argentines want the same things while thinking differently and promises to harness diversity without cancelling it.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: The movement competes in elections and the speech grounds legitimacy in the popular vote; lotteries for office are not part of its thinking.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The speech states that the state must be a slave of the law in confronting crime.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Governments restored price controls and subsidized food and utilities.

party-controls-media.rationale: The governments clashed with the Clarin group, using a media law and state advertising, but did not seek full control of all media.

party-commands-army.rationale: The speech wants the armed forces professionalized and committed to the role the Constitution gives them, not to a party.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the speech's praise of immigrant ancestors and the movement's welcoming migration policy.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Not addressed; adherents have no stated view and the party's leaders were not ascetic in pay.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: The party contained discipline-minded camps around the leader but also dissenting Peronists and allies, so adherents are split.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The speech wants a Mercosur with deeper institutional dimensions and new members.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The Argentine presidential system already gives this power, which the movement uses; not directly discussed.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The movement has no doctrine on church governance; the question is internal to Catholic or other churches.

clerical-rule.rationale: The governments legislated against the Catholic hierarchy's position on marriage and sexuality, so religious scholars do not hold authority in this view.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: The speech sets a national project and a professional military and lacks any internationalist anti-war doctrine of working-class defeatism.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Its liberal policy on sexuality and the arts is incompatible with moral censorship, though state media fights show some willingness to regulate.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Supporters proposed constitutional change enabling a third term and indefinite re-election though it never passed.

recall-officials.rationale: Not addressed; the speech speaks of citizen participation but offers no recall mechanism, and the movement governed under the existing system.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Argentina has no permanent military alliances now; the stance on alliances was non-aligned.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: The speech promises housing construction and access to decent homes, with no proposal to ban renting.

people-in-arms.rationale: The speech states the state has the monopoly of force and professional armed forces.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's industrial development and urban worker base suggest no moral preference for rural life.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Argentina is not a divided nation; the nearest analogue is the Malvinas claim, which the speech treats as a sovereignty issue.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The speech champions education and public school; no sign of anti-intellectualism.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The speech respects diversity and plural identities, from which relativism toward cultures is inferred, though not stated.

death-penalty.rationale: The movement's identity rests on prosecuting state killings of the dictatorship, and the speech ties crime to exclusion, making execution unlikely to be supported.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Under its health minister, the movement took a liberal approach to birth control and sexuality.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: The speech stresses educational quality and national planning of content, and the movement's liberal curriculum includes sex education; creationism is not in it.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the liberal line on sexuality and censorship wariness.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Argentina grants citizenship by birth in territory and the movement did not alter it.

minority-language-support.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the speech's respect for diversity and equal education from north to south.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Not addressed; adherents are likely split between pluralism and uniform secular laws.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the liberal legislation on marriage and gender identity that allowed unconventional lives.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: The speech says 'we are not the project of default' and seeks reduction and restructuring, not cancellation.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Economic independence was a core theme: freeing the economy from creditors and IMF conditions.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The speech works within the 1994 constitution and cites it as a source of legitimacy, but later governments floated constitutional changes, so adherents are split.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The speech ties progress to democracy and the rule of law, and the movement's growth model sought consumption and wages, not repression.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The movement was a recipient-country and wanted fair trade and debt relief, not aid per se.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The speech stresses multilateral law and a professional, development-oriented military; Argentina has no weapons programme and no source proposes one.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The movement won presidential elections by direct vote under the 1994 constitution and the speech grounds legitimacy in popular ratification.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Cristina Kirchner's bicentennial fund led to the removal of the central bank president, and governments used reserves for debt payment, treating the bank as an instrument of policy.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Not applicable beyond the Malvinas claim, which is a sovereignty dispute and not a peace deal.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The speech and constitutional references to social rights imply property is subject to social purpose, as in the Peronist social function tradition, and renationalizations followed.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A debate within Marxism that the movement never addressed.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Not documented; energy and mining expansion suggest limited precaution.

collective-defense.rationale: The speech opposes automatic alignments and Argentina belongs to no collective defence alliance, though it values multilateral law.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Consistent with its Malvinas stance on sovereignty and international law, but not discussed in the sources.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The movement clashed with the Church but did not move to curb its property or place clergy under state authority.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Argentina has an executive president and Kirchnerism's leaders led a party and movement; the idea of a nonpartisan symbolic head of state is foreign to it.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The speech seeks a unified federal nation; the question does not arise, so inferred.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Not addressed; Argentina is a federation and the movement stresses a national model with provincial coordination.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The speech says the era of predestined, fundamentalist and messianic leaders is over, which rules out sacral kingship.

flat-income-tax.rationale: The speech promises to make the tax system progressive and to broaden the tax base, so a single flat rate runs directly against it.

character-from-environment.rationale: The speech links crime to exclusion and inequality, implying circumstances shape people, though not a philosophical claim.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The speech says the state must be a slave of the law and that legal security applies to all.

space-expansion.rationale: Not discussed; inferred from the speech's priority on jobs, housing and basic services for the poor.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Not addressed; the movement works within a presidential republic.

leader-cult.rationale: Critics and scholars note personalism around the Kirchners, with public mass praise and imagery; adherents defend it as popular affection.

equal-parenting.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's gender equality stance and its support for women's rights groups pull in different ways.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: The question belongs to Marxist-Leninist debate and does not apply to the movement.

land-redistribution.rationale: Agrarian policy centred on export duties and conflict with farm exporters, not redistribution of estates.

refugee-return.rationale: Not addressed; no source states a position on refugees' return.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The speech rejects ultramontane nationalism and bases claims only on international law.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The governments legislated against Church doctrine and defended personal freedom in family law, so criminal punishment for leaving a religion is outside the movement.

women-must-cover.rationale: The movement's liberal legislation on sexuality and gender is incompatible with a legal dress mandate for women.

common-currency.rationale: The speech wants an exchange rate policy adapted to local productivity and Mercosur deepening, which cuts against a shared currency; not stated.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The speech aims at a united Latin America with Mercosur at its core, a union of peoples by language and history.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Not applicable; Argentina has no national-minority autonomy tradition and the sources do not address it.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Scholars describe the movement as developmentalist and not Marxist; not addressed.

ban-cartels.rationale: The speech targets concentrated economic groups and a regulatory state, and the governments had price agreements and a competition authority, but not a stated programme.

no-bailouts.rationale: Not addressed directly; the speech opposes adjustment for the poor and the financial rescue practices of the 1990s.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The 2013 judicial reform proposal was seen by critics as an attempt to bring the judiciary under the elected majority, which adherents defend as democratization.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Argentina's gender quota tradition and the movement's liberal gender approach support it, but no source states the exact policy.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: The speech says the project is not closed to the world and seeks market opening, and Mercosur integration.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: The speech notes that developed countries protect workers and industries, which supports labor standards in trade, but this is inferred.

moral-incentives.rationale: The speech ties social progress to effort and reward, with expanding consumption.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The speech opts for institutional change, though the 1970s Montoneros are a contested reference in the movement's memory.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The speech wants mobility through effort and capacity; not directly discussed.

history-own-civilization.rationale: The speech wants national identity and cultural unity through education.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The movement's anti-imperialism and its refusal of IMF and US pressure are the opposite of rule by advanced societies.

patriotic-education.rationale: The speech calls education a tool that builds national identity and unity.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the movement's inclusion agenda in general.

public-money-creation.rationale: Governments used central bank financing of the treasury, which links money creation to the state.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: The movement sought to rebuild a national capitalism with state support and did not predict collapse.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Not applicable; Argentina's own past empire is Spanish and the movement addressed Spain only as an economic partner.

delink-world-market.rationale: The speech says it is not about closing to the world and wants integration through Mercosur and open markets.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist thesis; the movement's labor politics is Peronist and treats union members as the core of the popular base.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The governments passed same-sex marriage and anti-discrimination law, which override owners' freedom to refuse service.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The speech roots rights in the Constitution, especially social rights in articles 14 and 14 bis.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the movement's Malvinas claim and anti-imperialism.

elective-rulers.rationale: The speech opens by saying the people exercised popular sovereignty in the April vote and builds legitimacy on ratification of the rulers.

minority-veto.rationale: The movement governed by majority rule in Congress and treated opposition obstruction as an obstacle, so individual consent vetoes are not part of it.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Not addressed; the speech stresses institutional respect and no one is above the law, but does not discuss resistance.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The movement worked with a strong presidency, so parliament supremacy is not a theme.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from general progressive social positions.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Not addressed; Argentina's beef and farming economy implies acceptance of use, with humane conditions.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The speech asks for solidarity but mainly through the state and taxation, not elite charity.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The speech says no change succeeds without citizens willing to participate actively, and calls on all to join the national project.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: The governments fought media groups, which suggests some sympathy, but the sources do not state this theory.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramscian readings are scholarly labels for Kirchnerism but adherents do not state the theory.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: The speech criticizes external indebtedness and the transfer of wealth to creditors and speculative groups.

native-born-offices.rationale: The speech honours immigrant ancestors and equality of all inhabitants, so reserving offices for the native-born is excluded.

party-own-road.rationale: The question is about communist parties and does not apply to the movement.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: The speech wants a model of its own and pay down debt, avoiding dependence on external financing.

return-lost-territory.rationale: The speech pledges to sustain the claim of sovereignty over the Malvinas.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Not addressed; no source indicates the movement sought such leadership.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Not stated; inferred from the movement's memory-and-justice politics about the dictatorship.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: The movement's prosecutions of dictatorship crimes rest on rejecting the idea that guerrillas and the state were symmetrical, which implies resisting such equivalences.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: A US historical question that the movement never addressed.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: The movement backed memorials at former detention centres and revision of the dictatorship era commemorations.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's gender policy focused on women and sexual diversity.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from its gender policy framing of violence against women.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Not addressed; the speech speaks of a model of its own for Argentina but stays within a Western constitutional framework.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The speech wants armed forces committed to the future and their constitutional role, and civilian control.

paid-care-work.rationale: Not covered in the sources; inferred from the movement's expansion of income transfers and its liberal gender agenda.

filial-duty.rationale: Not addressed; no source states a view on filial duty.

office-by-exam.rationale: Not addressed; the movement filled posts through party and electoral channels.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Renationalization of YPF and pension funds show a tendency to protect strategic sectors.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: The movement's liberal legislation on family and sexuality, including marriage equality, points to support for easy exit from marriage.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the representative electoral model the movement works in.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Cristina Kirchner nationalized the private AFJP pension funds, returning pensions to the state system.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Not part of the movement; it defends constitutional property rights while regulating them.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The speech commits to the Constitution and institutional quality, though governments often governed by decree.

single-official-language.rationale: Not addressed; Spanish is the de facto national language and the movement had no language policy.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Not covered in the sources; the movement's sovereignty focus points to support, while its pro-investment stance on strategic energy points the other way, so adherents are split.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Not addressed; US-style doctrine with no Argentine stance.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: The project explicitly puts expanding domestic consumption at the centre of growth.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: The speech commits to international law, multilateralism and respectful relations among states, which excludes funding foreign insurgents.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Contrary to the speech's commitment to international law and multilateralism.

corporate-influence.rationale: The speech says the 1990s state served concentrated economic groups with media echo.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Governments fought with media groups, but no documented NGO funding restriction.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Not addressed; the movement supported family allowances but also birth control access.

residents-only-property.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the movement's focus on national rather than local control.

job-guarantee.rationale: The speech promises genuine jobs through public works and unemployment subsidies, but not a legal guarantee.

democratic-peace.rationale: Not addressed; the movement supports democracy but did not promote it abroad.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The speech insists on strict compliance with the law everywhere and says governability cannot mean impunity.

non-intervention.rationale: The movement stressed respect for national sovereignty, although it accepted Haiti peacekeeping.

industrial-unions.rationale: Argentina's major unions are organized by industry and the movement allied with them.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The speech stresses an Argentina for all and respect for diversity, which excludes conspiracy theories about minorities.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: The governments extended legal marriage to same-sex couples, which affirms rather than abolishes its legal role.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The speech rejects dark agreements and demands transparent, rational rules, from which a right of access is inferred.

local-production.rationale: The speech wants domestic consumption and production and regional trade, but also export opening, so adherents are split.

informal-organisation.rationale: The movement is a large party and state-based formation and the governing coalition organized through the Justicialist Party.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Cristina Kirchner refused to recognize US court authority, though the speech claims respect for international law, so mixed.

religious-nation.rationale: The movement's pluralist approach and clashes with Church doctrine rule out a religiously defined nation.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Anti-US and anti-IMF rhetoric and refusal of automatic alignments are the opposite of ritual deference.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The speech promises a new revenue-sharing law to redistribute among provinces.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Not addressed; the movement supports private property alongside public services.

defeat-communism.rationale: The movement kept close ties with Cuba and Venezuela and opposed the US-led regional agenda, so it did not seek defeat of communism.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: The speech describes a health system uniting public, private and union sectors.

religion-illusion.rationale: The speech invokes God's help and the movement drew on Peronist Catholic social teaching, so religion is not regarded as an illusion.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The speech does not give a historical judgment but aims to rebuild capitalism as a source of mobility, from which a mildly positive view is inferred.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Not addressed as a structural claim; the movement's reforms focused on law and social policy.

socialized-care.rationale: Not addressed; the pension moratorium for homemakers is related but is not provision of care as a public service.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's cultural nationalism is civic and economic, with no language-purism programme, so a purge of loanwords is inferred as unwelcome.

treaties-binding.rationale: Not addressed; the movement never took a position on treaties with internal nations.

cooperative-communities.rationale: The project is national capitalism with a large state, not small self-governing communes.

majority-settlement.rationale: The speech celebrates diversity and equal opportunity across regions, so engineering settlement is not part of it.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The speech aims at a national capitalism with a state correcting its exclusions, rejecting both the deserter state and the omnipresent one.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Not addressed except the Malvinas claim, which the speech frames as sovereignty and not historical ethnic ties.

holocaust-denial.rationale: The movement's human rights politics rest on accepting documented state crimes, which excludes denial of historical atrocities.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The governments legalized same-sex marriage and are described as liberal on sexuality.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The speech calls for plural, diverse politics and rejects governability bought by pacts or impunity, although critics accuse the governments of pressuring opponents.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The governments openly overrode Church positions on marriage, and blasphemy punishment would conflict with their secular legislation.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The movement's anti-imperialist and anti-IMF stance rejects governing territories for the benefit of a ruling country.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: A religious doctrine that does not apply to the movement.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The movement is a secular-leaning electoral formation that legislated against Church positions.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The speech says that no leader can change things without a citizenry willing to participate, and calls for plural and transversal participation.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Not addressed as a theory, though policy joined class and gender concerns.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The movement took a liberal line on sexuality and gender policy, as shown by marriage equality, so legal recognition of gender identity fits its record even though the sources do not name it.

assisted-dying.rationale: Not addressed; adherents are split between liberal and Catholic positions.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The speech frames success from convictions on the left, and adherents identify against neoliberalism.

alienated-labor.rationale: The speech values work as the great social articulator, which cuts against a theory of alienation, but not directly discussed.

islam-incompatible.rationale: The speech's equality, diversity and anti-discrimination values exclude it, and the movement showed no such stance.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The speech places legitimacy in popular sovereignty and ratification by the people.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from gender policy and anti-impunity stance.

social-market-economy.rationale: The speech wants a market economy with a state that equalizes and a regulatory framework.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The speech wants armed forces that are professional, modern and committed to the future, and treats national defense as a state role.

rich-first.rationale: The speech rejects growth that excludes and demands distribution alongside growth.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: The speech says no automatic alignments should be expected and prefers multilateral relations with all.

state-harmful.rationale: The speech names the state as the great repairer of social inequality and as responsible for education, health and housing, so calling it unnecessary and harmful is the opposite of the project.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Kirchner's 2003 speech says debt cannot be paid at the cost of hunger and exclusion, and his government rejected an IMF structural adjustment programme and paid off the Fund.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Kirchnerism is a democratic party movement, though Cristina succeeded her husband Néstor in 2007 and the couple's family hold on the movement is criticised; adherents would not frame it as a hereditary right.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Inferred from a state-led developmentalism that relies on public banks and state credit rather than user-owned cooperative banks; the sources do not discuss mutual credit.

property-franchise.rationale: A Peronist, union-backed movement built on mass inclusion and human rights would reject any wealth test for voting; it extended votes to 16-year-olds in 2012.

domination-women-nature.rationale: The movement's feminism is a liberal rights agenda (marriage equality, gender identity, later abortion law) and the sources do not link it to a critique of the domination of nature; its extractive developmentalism cuts against it.

reification.rationale: Kirchnerism criticises neoliberal markets but is a Peronist, not Marxist, current and the sources never use this theory; adherents would be split or indifferent.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Inferred from the governments' fight with the Clarin group, which they cast as a concentrated corporate power distorting public debate; the claim is phrased in Marxist terms the movement does not use.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Kirchner's 2003 speech calls for the rule of law and an independent judiciary, though critics charge the governments with governing by emergency decree.

racial-franchise.rationale: The movement stands for universal suffrage and equal rights, and the 2003 speech centres inclusion and human rights; a racial limit on voting is foreign to it.

online-participation.rationale: The sources do not address internet participation; the movement favours mass mobilisation and parties, and adherents would be indifferent to online deliberation.

open-government-data.rationale: Inferred from the governments' transparency and access-to-information rhetoric and the 2016 law passed after them; the sources do not state a position.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The governments legalised same-sex marriage in 2010 over Church opposition, and nothing in Argentine Peronism supports restricting marriage between faiths.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Targeting a religious minority's shops contradicts the movement's human rights and anti-discrimination stance.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; the movement prefers party and union mobilisation, so adherents would be neither for nor against sortition-based assemblies.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Kirchnerism is largely secular in policy but not anti-religious, and it takes no position on how religions should interpret their own doctrine.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Kirchnerism treated redistribution and a strong state as counterweights to concentrated economic power, as the 2003 address and its record of price controls and transfers show.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: The governments' liberal turn on sexuality, including the 2010 same-sex marriage law, makes open service by gay and lesbian people consistent with the movement's record.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Kirchnerism was a Peronist movement operating alongside a Catholic majority and never sought to promote unbelief through public schools.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Inferred: the governments pursued human rights prosecutions and kept conventional policing, with no support for abolition.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Inferred: the movement is a majoritarian electoral coalition with no record of backing guaranteed community shares of executive power.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Kirchnerism centred on state provision, from public health to social transfers and subsidised services, rather than leaving help for the poor to charities.

term-limits.rationale: Cristina Kirchner's circle sought to keep re-election open and the movement relied on long-serving leaders; inferred, not from a stated position on term limits.

vote-delegation.rationale: Inferred: the movement works through party and union structures and has not backed revocable vote delegation.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Kirchnerism never addressed the issue and nothing in its principles settles it.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Inferred from the movement's liberal social turn, though its Catholic-rooted Peronist wing would be less sure.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The governments' marriage equality and civil code reforms rest on equality between spouses, in line with the movement's liberal turn on marriage.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Inferred from the movement's inclusive, regional-integration outlook and its liberal social turn; no source addresses local voting by foreign residents.

rent-control.rationale: Inferred from the state-led model with price controls and protective intervention (s2); rent caps specifically are not discussed in the sources.

abolish-ip.rationale: Inferred: the model favoured protected national industry and state development rather than abolishing property forms, and the sources never address patents.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Inferred from the movement's human rights framing against the dictatorship; its youth organising (La Cámpora) was political, not drilled national-service training.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Inferred from Argentina's non-proliferation stance and Latin American integration; the sources say nothing direct.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Inferred from the movement's anti-imperialist, sovereignty-centred rhetoric and Latin American integration (s2); foreign bases are not discussed.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Inferred from the movement's central human rights policy of prosecuting dictatorship crimes (s2, s5); recognition of other genocides is not covered in the sources.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The movement's Peronist developmentalism stresses labour, unions, wage recovery and social transfers over rentier and financial returns.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Inferred: nothing in the sources supports pacifism, and a mainstream Peronist movement would accept self-defence.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Peronist national narratives stress historical continuity, but the sources do not address this and adherents are not clearly committed to the strong claim.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: The movement's gender-identity law (s2, later phase) implies openness, but adherents are likely split on the academic claim that sex itself is constructed.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: The gender-identity law points one way, but a movement with a strong women's-rights and abortion-rights wing is not committed to this theoretical claim.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: The movement honours victims of the dictatorship and its own dead, but not as saints; the sacral wording makes agreement uncertain.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Inferred: the movement frames politics as a struggle over distribution and national projects, not a spiritual war of good and evil.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Inferred: the movement is territorial-civic and has no diaspora-homeland doctrine.

culture-before-state.rationale: Inferred: Kirchnerism is built on state action first (state-led developmentalism, s2), so culture-before-state is contrary to its approach.

god-not-male.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's liberal social turn sits alongside a Catholic-identified base, so adherents are likely split.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Inferred: the movement is secular-political and does not judge religious texts by a feminist test; Catholic-identified adherents would reject it.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Inferred: the movement stresses national economic sovereignty, but through state and national capital rather than ethnic or majority-group ownership.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Inferred: Argentine federalism and provincial structure are not organised by peoples and the movement has no such programme.

independent-unions.rationale: Inferred from the movement's close alliance with Peronist unions and union backing for its governments (s2), which ties unions to the ruling party.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Kirchnerism is a state-led developmentalist movement that never claimed to be socialist, so it has no stance on what counts as socialism.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Kirchner's 2003 speech centres the public hospital, and later governments renationalised privatised utilities as part of the anti-neoliberal turn.

second-chamber.rationale: Inferred: the movement worked within Argentina's bicameral federal Congress and never proposed abolishing the Senate.

municipal-property.rationale: Inferred from a developmentalism built on the national state and national capitalism rather than community ownership.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Inferred from a strongly centralised, presidency-led movement that did not favour decision-making by local assemblies.

family-wage.rationale: Inferred from the Peronist tradition of wage rises and social transfers meant to support working households, which the movement continued.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Inferred from a state-regulation-minded approach that stressed public provision of medicines, not deregulation.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Inferred from the governments' expansion of public science funding; ageing research itself is not addressed in the sources.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Inferred from a state-led economic model with currency and capital controls that sought to keep payments visible to the state.

online-anonymity.rationale: The movement has no documented position on online anonymity and its adherents are not clearly aligned either way.

person-over-state.rationale: Inferred from its human rights prosecutions and rights-expanding laws, though the Peronist tradition also stresses the community.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Not addressed; the movement is secular in government, with Catholic and non-religious adherents alike.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Inferred: Argentina's provinces hold constitutionally entrenched powers and Kirchnerism pressed federal control mainly through funding, not by revoking them.

gm-crops.rationale: Inferred from the governments' reliance on soy exports and the farm sector's genetically modified soy, which they taxed rather than restricted.

dense-cities.rationale: Not addressed in the sources and no clear position follows from the movement's principles.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Inferred from a national-popular framing organised around class and nation, with anti-discrimination policy rather than racial organising.

racial-pride.rationale: Not addressed by the sources and no position follows from the movement's principles.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Inferred from the 2003 speech's pursuit of the Malvinas claim by diplomacy and a defensive role for the armed forces.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Kirchnerism stresses Latin American integration and national sovereignty but the sources do not discuss language as defining a nation; split.

communal-electorates.rationale: Kirchnerism is a secular-liberal state movement with a liberal turn on marriage and sexuality; separate religious electorates are foreign to Argentina and not stated, so inferred.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Kirchner's 2003 speech and later governments cast creditors, the IMF and foreign interests as threats to national sovereignty, though not partition specifically.

free-public-college.rationale: The governments expanded university access and public education spending, and Argentine public universities already charge no tuition, which the movement defended.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Kirchnerism relied on export duties and energy subsidies and has no defined stance on pollution taxes; split.

future-generations.rationale: Not a central theme in the sources; a broadly shared centre-left view, inferred.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Later phases advanced gender-equality laws and a ministry for women and gender, but the care-values claim is not stated in the sources; inferred.

arms-reduction.rationale: Kirchnerism stressed human rights and regional integration but kept defence spending with no stated line on arms reduction; split.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; the movement favoured transparency rhetorically but no stated line on secret treaties.

capital-controls.rationale: The governments imposed foreign-exchange and capital restrictions in the later Fernandez de Kirchner years as part of its anti-neoliberal, state-led model.

missingStatements.text: Governments should refuse austerity programs imposed by the IMF and repay external debt only on terms that protect domestic growth.
missingStatements.rationale: Kirchner's 2003 speech says debt cannot be paid at the cost of hunger and exclusion, and his government rejected an IMF structural adjustment programme and paid off the Fund.

missingStatements.text: Private creditors of a defaulted government should accept a large reduction in what they are owed.
missingStatements.rationale: The speech sets reduced debt amounts, lower interest and longer maturities as the aims of negotiation, and the 2005 restructuring followed, with later refusal of holdout demands.
missingStatements.declined: Narrow Argentine debt-restructuring episode; the general stance is captured by refuse-lender-austerity.

missingStatements.text: Governments should tax agricultural exports to fund social spending and keep domestic food prices down.
missingStatements.rationale: The 2008 farm export duty plan and the soy export tax are described as core instruments of the model, funding redistribution and prompting months of protest.
missingStatements.declined: Specific agrarian export-tax instrument; too niche for the shared bank.

missingStatements.text: The state should break up concentrated private media ownership by law.
missingStatements.rationale: Cristina Kirchner's government fought the Clarin group with a media law and state advertising, a conflict at the centre of the movement.

notes: Positions on abortion and gender identity come mostly from the 2019-2023 Frente de Todos phase, and Nestor Kirchner himself was reportedly cautious on abortion. Personalism around the Kirchners and the status of anti-corruption claims are contested, so those answers are low confidence. Many answers on religion, language, animals and Marxist theory are inferred from the movement's general stance.
